text: Given an m by n integer matrix, return the length of the longest strictly increasing path. From each cell you may move up, down, left, or right — no diagonals, and no wrapping around the edges.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — strictly increasing means each step goes to a strictly larger value, so equal neighbours don't connect? Length counts cells, so a single cell has length one? And the matrix is never empty?
Correct on all three. Strictly larger, length is the number of cells, and the matrix always has at least one cell.

Let me run through the example. Nine, nine, four; six, six, eight; two, one, one gives four, via one, two, six, nine up the left side. The strictly part is doing real work here — those equal ones, sixes and nines don't chain together.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would run a plain DFS from every cell and explore every increasing path. Paths share long tails, so that's exponential. This problem reminds me of longest path in a directed acyclic graph. Draw an edge from each cell to every strictly larger neighbour. Every step strictly increases the value, so you can never return to a cell you've left — that would need a value greater than itself. So the graph is a DAG. That matters: longest path in a general graph is NP-hard, but in a DAG it's polynomial. So the natural framing is DP: dp of r, c is the length of the longest increasing path starting at r, c.
Do you need a visited array to avoid cycles, like a normal DFS?

No — and that's a direct consequence of the DAG property. The DFS only ever moves to strictly larger cells, so it cannot revisit a cell on the current path. Strictness does the job a visited array normally does. Adding one would actually be wrong — different start cells share tail segments, and those tails should be reused. I let memoization handle the reuse, not a visited flag that would block it.

Here's the plan. There are two clean versions, both order m n. One: top-down, dp of a cell is one plus the max dp over its strictly larger neighbours, and the answer is the max over all cells. Two: bottom-up, count each cell's strictly smaller neighbours, then peel the zero in-degree cells layer by layer; the number of layers is the answer. Three: I'll code the memoized DFS first, since it's shorter, then show the peel. One thing worth flagging — without the memo, the DFS is exponential because paths re-explore shared tails. With it, each cell is computed once: m n cells times four neighbours. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. The main function calls the DFS from every cell and keeps the best. The DFS returns the cached value if there is one; otherwise it starts at one for the cell itself, tries all four directions, and for every in-bounds neighbour that is strictly larger, takes one plus that neighbour's answer. Then it writes the result back into the memo. One thing worth flagging — memo equal to zero is a safe not-computed sentinel, because every real answer is at least one, so zero can never be a valid cached value.
You mentioned a bottom-up version. When would you prefer it?

When I'm worried about recursion depth. The DFS recurses as deep as the longest path, which for a snake-shaped matrix is order m n and can blow the stack. The Kahn version is iterative — no recursion at all. It's standard Kahn topological sort, but instead of recording an order, I count layers. In-degree is the number of strictly smaller neighbours, so the sources are local minima. The easy-to-get-wrong part is the edge direction: count smaller neighbours, but relax toward larger ones. A cell is peeled only once all its smaller neighbours are gone, so its layer equals the longest chain ending at it — and the total layer count is the answer.

Let's dry-run the memo version on the example; expected four. The nines are peaks, so their dp is one, and a six next to a nine gets two. The row that matters is the bottom one: the middle one steps to the two, then the six, then the nine, so its dp is four — the max. The four sits on the smallest cell, which makes sense: dp is how far I can still go. That matches. Corner cases: three, four, five; three, two, six; two, two, one gives four. A single cell gives one. An all-equal matrix gives one, since no step is allowed.

Let me think about complexity here. Both are order m n time and order m n space — each cell processed once, four neighbours each. Oh, one more thing — the two versions compute opposite ends of the same chain. The memo stores how far forward from here, so its max sits on the minimum cell; the Kahn layer stores how far I've come, so its max sits on the maximum cell. Same chain length, read from either end. And the strict comparison is load-bearing: with non-decreasing moves, equal neighbours would form cycles and it would stop being a DAG. The DFS would recurse forever, and the peel would never free those cells.

Excellent. Three things stood out. You identified the DAG structure and used it to justify both no visited array and polynomial time — most people just assert it's DP. You gave two approaches and knew exactly when the iterative one earns its keep. And you spotted that strictness is what keeps it acyclic. Strong hire.
